caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 380 of 1965.
lawyer:
A.T. M. Kamrul Islam ------- For Appellant.
B.N. Chowdhury ------- For Respondent.
parties:
Osman Ali Talukder ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Sukumar Majumder  ------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
This appeal, by defendant No.1; is directed against the decision of the Subordinate Judge, Bogra, in Title Appeal No. 36 of 1963 reversing that of the Munsif, 3rd Court, Bogra in Title Suit No. 183 of 1961.

2. The plaintiff respondents filed a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit land by evicting the defendants. The plaintiffs' case, in short is that the suit land was recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 160 of mouza Borai and the plaintiffs, by an amicable partition amongst themselves and pro-defendants, were possessing the same; that during the last c.s. operation Jasmat Sardar  was possessing the suit land as a barga darunder Girish Chandra and others, the plaintiffs predecessors, on delivering half of the produce of the land from year to year; and that during Jasmat Sardar's life time the land was taken and given borga bandabosta to others. As Jasmat was possessing the land as borgadar his name was wrongly recorded in the C.S. record as tenant paying borga rent though he was never recognized as a tenant by the plaintiffs' predecessors. Acting on rumors, that lands recorded in the names of bargadars paying half the produce as rent, had vested in the bargadar's ; defendants, 1, 2, and 3, got fraudulent kabala from Jasmat's daughters, defendants 4 and 5 and forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff's from the suit land in Baishak, 1364 B.S. and hence the suit.

3. Defendant 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement where he stated, inter alia, that Jasmat Sardar was a recorded occupancy raiyat and defendants 3, 4 and 5 were the heirs of Jasmat Sardar  and he derived good title by purchase from them. His further case is that the landlords were present at the time of the preparation of the settlement records, that neither Jasmat nor his heirs over gave up possession of the land and the plaintiff never possessed the land by their borgadars, that during the revisional settlement operation the suit land had been recorded in the names of defendants 3,4 and 5 and they possessed the same on payment of money rent and that the suit was barred by limitation.

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the suit after finding that the C.S. record (Ext. 2) indicated that Jasmat Sardar has acquired a tenancy right in the suit land and that there was no evidence that during his life the land was taken back from him and given to some other persons as borga by the plaintiffs predecessors, that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the date of the institution of the suit.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge reversed the decision of the trial Court after finding that the C.S. recorded was not correctly recorded, and Jasmat was a borgadar and he was in possession till his death, 6/7 years back, and hence the suit was within 12 years of possession of the last recorded borgadar, and the transferee-defendants had no saleable interest in the suit land and as such the defendants were liable to be evicted.

6. Mr. A.T.M. Kamrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge misinterpreted the decision in the case of Kumir Mondal Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury (1962) in 14 DL:R 801 in as much as the principle laid down in the said case is that a borgadar recorded in the C.S. Khatian as tenant before the introduction of the proviso to clause (17) of section 3 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 by the amending Act of 1928 can plead tenancy right even after the introduction of the proviso. He has further submitted that the presumption of correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian cannot be held to have been rebutted merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entry. Mr. Islam, in support of his contention, has relied on Alimuddin Munshi Vs. Mainuddin Talukdar (1962) 14 DLR 725.

7. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondent has submitted that the presumption of the correctness of the record of right has been lost by passage of time, and that where it is on record that Jasmat Sardar  gave kabuliyat to the landlords as a borgadar before the preparation of the C.S. record and there is no other evidence that there had been any other agreement creating a tenancy in favor of Jasmat Sardar  the C.S. record must be held to have been wrongly prepared.

8. The case of Kumir Mondal and ors Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and ors (1962) 14 DLR 801 went up to the Pakistan Supreme Court and the decisionis reported in 17 DLR (SC) at 392. After referring to the history of the legislation of the Bengal Tenancy(Amendment) Act, 1928 and a number of decisions of the Calcutta High Court as well as of the Dacca High Court the Pakistan Supreme Court held:

"that this proviso does not debar a person against whom a suit is now filed for recovery of a share of the crop as a bargadar, to set up the defense that he is not a bargadar but a tenant. In such a suit the presumption of correctness of the record of rights may also be invoked in aid as a circumstances supporting the defense but this will certainly not be a conclusive presumption. The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103 -B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this that the entry in the record of right represents the correct stale of affairs on the elate that it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs is continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section; but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is its presumptive value. This is a matter therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof".

9. The C.S. Khatian recorded Jasmat Sardar  as a borgadar as well as a rayotisthitiban under Girish Chandra Majumdar and others at a rental of half of the produces inclusive of cess. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that Jasmat took borga settlement by a kabuliyat (Ext. 1) for a term of 7 years from 1321 B.S. and the preparatory works of C.S. operation started in the locality after 1327 B.S. and the record of rights was finally published in 1925 corresponding to 1332 B.S. He has observed that "it is quite likely that the settlement operation actually began at a stage when the term of the barga lease did not expire. It is, therefore, clear borga has been mentioned in the khatian. In the absence of any other stipulation between the parties Jasmat would be deemed to have continued in possession as a borgadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in section 116 of the T.P. Act and as enunciated in principle in section 51 B.T. Act".

10. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has empathetically urged that a finding as to the rebuttal of a statutory presumption is a finding of a fact and cannot be challenged in second appeal. In support of his contention he has referred 10 Aminuddin Biswas Vs. Miajan Biswas, (1960) 12 DLR 103, CharuBalaRudra Vs. Narayan Prosad Sen(1962) 14 DLR 159 and Dabiruddin Molla Vs. Prem Dasi(1967) 19 DLR 371.

<u>11. A finding as to a rebuttal of a statutory presumption is no doubt a finding of fact and it should not ordinarily be disturbed in second appeal. In the present case, however, the finding as to the rebuttal of the presumption of the C,S. record is based on a material mistaken assumption that Jasrnat Sardar would be deemed to have continued in possession as a bargadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and as enunciated in principle under section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has conceded that neither section 166 of the Transfer of Property Act nor section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is applicable to a bargadar. He has, however, contended that the principle of holding over has been applied by way of analogy. The right of holding over, unless conferred by a statute, cannot be implied or inferred by analogy. Long five years after the terms of the borga kabuliyat expired, the C.S. Khatian was published on 6-9-25. The assumption of the Court of appeal below that the settlement operation actually began at the stage when the terms of the borga lease did not expire is based on no evidence.</u>

12. Again the learned Subordinate Judge seems to have proceeded on the view that the term 'borgadar' itself is a negation of the right of tenancy. I may refer to the following observation made by D.C. Bhattacharya, J. In Soda Mia Vs. MomrajBhuiya(1974) 26 DLR 245.

"It has not been defined anywhere what a 'bargadar is? We find in Wilson's Glossaries, that the term 'barga' has been defined as an agreement by which the cultivator engages to pay the landlord half of the produce, the latter providing half of the seed and paying the whole of the rent, from the definition of 'tenant' as given in section 3, . clause (17) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, as it stood before the amendment of 1929, we find that a tenant means a person who holds land under another person, and is, or but for a special contract would be liable to pay rent for that land to that person, and in clause (13) of the same section 'rent' has been defined as whatever is lawfully payable or deliverable in money or kind by a tenant to his landlord on account of the use or occupation of the land held by the tenant, So we find that there is nothing in clause (13), or clause (17) of section 3 which militates against a bargadar being a tenant, Rent, according to clause (13) of section 3 as we have seen may be in money or in kind and it need not be a fixed amount, there is nothing in law to prevent a landlord from accepting a variable or fluctuating quantity of the produce of land as rent, Therefore, according to the provisions of law, as were in force before 1929, there was nothing inherently inconsistent between the characters of a bargadarand a tenant, "

13, In 1929 by an amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the Legislature sought to bring about a certain change with regard to presumption about the status of a person who used to cultivate lands under barga system, by adding the following provision to the definition of 'tenant' to section 3(17) of B,T. Act.

"Provided that a person who, under the system generally known as adhi, bargaor bhag cultivates the land of the produce to that person, is not a tenant, unless

(i) Such person has been expressly admitted to be a tenant by his landlord in any documents executed by him or executed in his favor and accepted by him, or

(ii) he has been or is held by a Civil Court to be a tenant."

14. Hamoodur Rahman, J. as he was then, delivering the judgment in the case of Promotha Nath Chowdhury and others Vs, Kumir Mondal and others observed as follows:

"It seems to us that the only change that the Legislature has labored to bring about is 10 lay down that; only in the first instance there will be a presumption 'that" a person holding under a system of adhi, barga or bhogis not a tenant, but this presumption will be rebutted only if it is established that he has been admitted by the landlord to be a tenant or is declared in a previous suit to be a tenant or if he can in a suit where this question is put in issue establish status as such tenant, In effect it seems that the Legislature has labored in in vain or worse avoided its responsibility and really thrown the burden upon the Court to resolve this question, for the net result appears, in substance, to leave the question where it was, apart from shifting the burden of proof on the tenant. To this extent possibly there has been a departure from the old principle."

Thus even after the amendment a bargadar can raise a contention in any suit that he is a tenant.

15. In Alimuddin Munshi Vs. Mainuddin Talukdar (1962) 14 DLR 725 it has been held:

“Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the 'record-or-rights, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of section l03(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records-of-rights. There mutbe further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may be to show that the presumption has been rebutted. "

The learned Subordinate Judge has not adverted to this case, though relied on by the learned Munsif. For want of proper approach to the material question in the matter and non-appreciation of the evidence on the records particularly the evidence of the D.Ws. he has arrived at an erroneous decision. In the present case, apart from merely asserting that the C.S. Khatian was 'Wrongly recorded, the plaintiff did not adduce any other evidence in support of his contention. There was no averment that Jasmat continued to possess the land on the expiry of the terms of the kabuliyat on the same terms and conditions. In fact there is no mention of a borga kabuliyat in the plaint. On the other hand, defendant No.1, apart from relying on the C.S. record, produced Defendant 2, the Tahsildar of the landlords, who stated that at the time of C.S. operation he himself and another amin looked after the preparation of the C.S. record and the suit land belonged to Jasmat on payment of paddy lent to the landlords. This witness admitted the kabuliyat to be written in his hand. He further stated in cross-examination that he held some lands of the landlords as bargadar but his name was recorded as mere borgadar possessor with an entry in the rent column.

16. I, therefore, hold that the presumption of correctness of the C.S. record has not been rebutted in this case. The next question is whether the presumptive value of the C.S. record, under section 114 of the Evidence Act, has been destroyed in this case or whether its presumptive value is still available to defendant 1.

The suit is of 1961. Instead of remanding the case I think I should dispose of this appeal under section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

17. D.W. 1 Osman Ali, stated that Jasmat possessed the land as tenant and after his death his heirs defendants 3,4 and 5 got the suit land ; that he purchased the interest of defendants 3, 4 and 5 by registered kabalas Ext. 1 and l(a); that the suit land was at first recorded in the names of defendants 3, 4 and 5 and the Majumdar landlords filed an objection, under section 19(1) of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and got their names recorded but the defendants, 3, 4 and 5 preferred an appeal, under section 19(2) of the said Act, and the land was again in their names. Ext. C is the certified copy of that judgment of the appellate officer. The Government also collected rent from the defendant No. 4 vide Ext. B Defendant's categorical statement that Jasmat got tenancy right in the suit land and after his death his heirs were possessing the same before his purchase are corroborated by D.W. 2 Haji Monsurulla, the tahsildar and D.W. 2 Majan Shah who held land contiguous to the suit land.

18. P.W. 1 is the only witness on behalf of the plaintiffs. He stated that the suit land was taken from Jasmat and was given borgabandabast to others. He did not state who used to cultivate the land after Jasmat but merely stated that when the defendant disposed the plaintiff Morlan Shah was the bargadar. Madan Shah according to D.Ws. 1 and 3 left for India long ago. Though P.W. 1 stated he had an account book for borga receipts he neither produced the account book nor any borga receipt. In the present case the presumptive value of the C.S. record under section 114 of the Evidence Act must be held to be still available to contesting defendant.

19. From the evidence on record it is clear that the predecessors of Defendant 1 never possessed the land as a bargadar of the plaintiffs and the defendant’s assertion that Jasmat and his heirs possessed the land in their own rights has been amply substantiated by the evidence on record. From Ext. 1it cannot be said, though contended by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, that the subsequent possession of Jasmat was one of a bargadar . I do not find any mention of the kabuliyat in the C.S. Khatian. The learned Subordinate Judge has assumed, on a total misrepresentation of evidence on the record, that since Jasmat died 6/7 years back the sui t is within twelve years of possession through a recorded bargadar. From the evidence on record it is clear that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the institution of suit. The learned Munsif rightly dismissed the suit.

20. In the result, the appeal succeeds and is hereby allowed. The decision of the learned Subordinate Judge is set aside and that of learned Munsif is restored. There will, however, be no order as to costs.

End.
